articles.title: Nathan Vass’ Deciding to See: Washington State Book Awards Finalist
articles.author: Nathan Vass
paras: We urban planning and transit enthusiasts tend not to think of the street in terms of narrative. Most of the literature we digest on these favorite subjects of ours – the opening of a new train line, the behind-the-scenes of a housing development, the political importance of this or that measure and its effects – is in the form of articles or video essays, which have the luxury of being instantly producible, with up-to-the-minute observations and (ideally) journalism’s commitment to a minimum of editorializing. We think of journalism as the primary method of which to conceive of the street.

A 300-page book which took five years to write might seem an odd fit for the above landscape, especially a book that can’t be called journalism, even if it is nonfiction. But I think humans ultimately conceive of everything in terms of narrative.

We think of our days and our projects and our entire lives as stories, with arcs, in which we (of course) are the protagonist. We wish for happy endings, or at least edifying ones, and if we don’t get them we tell ourselves the story isn’t over yet. We are linear, time-based creatures, and in the same way we search for a story when watching one of the time-based art forms, even when there may not be one there at all (like dance), we frame how we think about our lives using the rules of narrative.

I think stories are the most powerful way to communicate. Paul Currington says opinions divide people; stories bring them together. In our (dis)information age, facts, or assertions masquerading as facts, have shown themselves to have limited value in changing minds.

If your family member is prejudiced, they won’t come around to your perspective when you dump data in their lap explaining how racism or sexism are shortsighted. They’ll come around because of primary experience happening in the one story they do care about, their own , the story of their life, as they get to know their coworker who’s from somewhere far away, or their friend’s child, who lives by different rules. The human element.

I didn’t write either of my books to change people’s minds. I wrote them to share a world I find interesting and underrepresented in the world of literature. I wrote them because there was so much life happening in this “lowbrow” space of unglamorous liminal life, so dense with incident and color and laughter and sorrow, and so few artists were transposing it to the “highbrow” space of probing literary reflection, of the word as art form.

I know there are others like me, but maybe too many of our great authors stay inside their offices, and too many of our best bus drivers don’t study comparative literature. Can I help it if I have interests and passions which have nothing to do with each other??

We know the power of stories, and we know the joy of sharing bus stories, which we humans will never stop telling each other, not as long as there’s transit in our lives. I’m frankly floored by the success my latest book continues to have – continuously bestselling in our city for over a year now, taught as a textbook at Seattle U, and now a Finalist for the 2026 Washington State Book Awards , alongside Rebecca Brown (Eep eep! I can die happy now) and others… all of this is thanks to you readers and enthusiasts, especially transit enthusiasts.

The Urbanist 's readers are my ideal audience: those of us interested in living as an urban collective, curious to see how the world of the street looks when viewed through the lens of art and narrative, searching for how we can live in the same forward direction, part of the same common project.
More press and interviews about the book here . Buy the book anywhere books are sold, including our own Elliott Bay Books, where I recently signed all copies :)

articles.title: Washington climate tech founders score funding as AI boom drains investor cash
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: Some climate tech startups tied to the AI boom are still attracting investors, but deals are fewer overall and times are tougher for companies addressing sustainability issues that don’t align with data center needs.

Concerns about those trends inspired a one-time Washington state initiative called the Opalene Climate Challenge , which was led by the nonprofit VertueLab . The effort announced six investments from a pool of nearly 40 applicants.

The program planned to partner with the state to secure matching dollars, but organizers realized it would take too long to raise the needed capital. Instead, they relied solely on philanthropic donors.

“The imperative was to get the money out to these climate tech startups who are doing extraordinary work but are confronting that pinch in capital,” said Allison Arnold, co-director of the Opalene Climate Challenge.

Sustainability startups that develop hardware or physical products can face a more difficult path to scale than software companies because they typically require more capital, longer development cycles and time-consuming work to manufacture, test and deploy their technologies.

The challenge aimed to fill an early-stage funding gap with recoverable grants from donor-advised funds. Successful investments will return proceeds to the donor’s fund or another designated nonprofit.

Five of the six winners are commercializing technologies developed at the University of Washington or Washington State University. Many of the startups have participated in mentoring programs such as the Cascadia Clean Tech Accelerator or UW’s CoMotion Labs Climate Tech Incubator, or received investments from the E8 angel group.

“Those entrepreneurs who have actively sought out the resources in our ecosystem have had greater success. For most companies, it takes more than just the money,” Arnold said. At the same time, she added, “money is what has been missing in our corner of the country. We don’t have the type of risk capital that’s available in places like Silicon Valley, Boston or New York.”

articles.title: Seattle and San Francisco: Big tech, political backlash and the AI boom
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Tech remade Seattle and San Francisco over the past three decades, bringing jobs and wealth along with soaring housing costs and a political backlash. Now the AI boom is hitting both cities, before either has resolved the tensions that have repeatedly divided their communities.

That’s the subject of this week’s GeekWire Podcast, a live joint taping with the Blue City Blues podcast at the National Nordic Museum in Seattle. GeekWire co-founder John Cook joins historian Margaret O’Mara, author of “ The Code ,” and San Francisco journalist Jonathan Weber, author of “ City on the Edge ,” with Blue City Blues hosts David Hyde and Sandeep Kaushik.
Here are some of the key takeaways from the conversation.
The tech industry’s conflicts in Seattle and San Francisco began when the industry moved out of the suburbs and into the middle of both cities.
Silicon Valley grew up 30 to 40 miles south of San Francisco, and Microsoft built a suburban campus in Redmond that O’Mara called “its own kind of bubble far away from the city.”

When Weber arrived in San Francisco in 1990 to cover Silicon Valley for the Los Angeles Times, he said, “there was essentially no tech in the city at all.” That changed with the dot-com boom, which brought the first backlash in San Francisco’s Mission District in the late 1990s.

In Seattle, a similar shift happened with Amazon’s move to South Lake Union, starting in 2010. John said Amazon was “most perfectly positioned” at its earlier headquarters on Beacon Hill, southeast of downtown Seattle, “completely isolated from the rest of the city.”

“When things really shifted for Amazon is when they decided to plant themselves in the middle of the city,” John said. “Then things accelerate, and then these problems start to come in, and Amazon starts to get blamed.”
The tech industry grew up in an era of low taxes and light regulation, and that’s baked into its business model.

O’Mara pointed to 1978, when California voters passed Proposition 13, which capped property taxes and “essentially starved localities of revenue,” she said. Personal computers and video games were taking off in that same era. “Silicon Valley’s kind of grown up in that world,” she said.

In Seattle, John said, Amazon’s view was that it was doing enough by bringing jobs to the city, while the city’s progressive leaders wanted more as prices rose. “Those two philosophies just collided in Seattle in real time,” he said.
Cities have limited leverage, Weber said. “A company can move two miles and avoid whatever taxes the city wants to impose.”
Seattle’s tech and business leaders, unhappy with the city’s political leadership, are organizing to fill the gap themselves.

Asked whether tech leaders think they’ve been getting good leadership from Seattle’s mayors, John said, “Short answer: No.” Businesses feel they’re paying a growing list of new taxes, he said, without seeing results on basics like potholes and clean streets.

In recent months, business figures including Microsoft’s Brad Smith, former Gov. Chris Gregoire and Joe Nguyen of the Seattle Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce have started forming coalitions and pooling their resources. “They’re going on offense,” John said. “They feel there’s a vacuum and a gap here based on this lack of political leadership.”
John said one of a mayor’s big jobs is to be “the chief cheerleader of the region and the city,” and Seattle’s recent mayors haven’t done it.
Weber said San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie has made that role a big part of his success: “Even though he’s a billionaire, he comes across as kind of a regular San Francisco guy.”
“That’s kind of a regular San Francisco guy these days,” O’Mara quipped.
San Francisco is the center of the AI boom, but Seattle and the Bay Area have always depended on each other more than they’ve competed.
Weber called San Francisco the undisputed capital of AI, as the home of OpenAI and Anthropic. The boom has brought so much wealth to the city, he said, that “there’s a mansion shortage.”

John said the gap between the two regions in venture funding for AI is “an astronomical difference.” But OpenAI and Anthropic have both opened engineering centers in the Seattle area, he said, hiring people who don’t want to leave.
Microsoft and Amazon both raised early money from Bay Area venture capitalists, O’Mara said.

John cited the longtime advice for Seattle founders: “Start your company and build your company in Seattle, raise your money in the Bay Area.” But Seattle has always run second to the Bay Area, John said, and that’s OK. “Who cares?” he said. “They are their own thing. We’re our own thing.”
The Gilded Age offers a precedent for putting guardrails on AI.

O’Mara compared the moment to the era of Carnegie and Rockefeller, when fast-growing industries overwhelmed a small U.S. government, and the regulation that followed still left room to make a lot of money.
Overemphasizing the novelty of AI, she said, “becomes a very convenient excuse not to regulate it.”

Weber said the AI debate is hard to read because most of the people in it are “talking their book,” with a business interest in the positions they take. The issue is arising, he said, at a time when “we essentially don’t have any national political leadership that’s able to deal with it.”
“So many things are indeed new,” O’Mara said, “but it doesn’t mean that nothing can be done.”
Both cities need to protect their quality of place, and tech itself can undermine it.

O’Mara said building a tech hub comes down to three things: capital, institutions such as research universities, and quality of place. Asked what Seattle and San Francisco should do differently over the next decade, she picked the third.
“This is not just making things nice for Amazon engineers getting paid $300,000 a year,” O’Mara said. “It is making the city safe, vital and fun.”

Weber said tech threatens that sense of place, because people who can shop, meet and find entertainment online don’t need the city in the same way. In San Francisco’s traditional nightlife districts, he said, there’s little going on after 9 p.m., while the city’s caterers and party planners are busy. “A lot of social life has moved indoors into private spaces,” he said.
To which John joked, “I just want to enjoy San Francisco in the metaverse.”

articles.title: Op-Ed: Fill in the Spring Boulevard Gap with a Trail
articles.author: Eastside Urbanism
paras: Do arterial roads belong in city parks? That is one of the key questions the Bellevue City Council will need to consider during its October 6 budget deliberations on transportation projects. The staff has presented an option to give full funding (for the first time) of $74.8 million to the one-third-mile, two-lane Spring Boulevard “gap” with a new 0.1% sales tax . But this "Zone 3" plan is colliding with another emerging project on the same land: the BelRed Neighborhood Park .

We believe roads like that do not belong in a park. The City should instead plan a pedestrian/bicycle-only trail. But before we make that case, let’s step back to understand the historical precedents and the reasons the City wants to build the road.

Bellevue, the self-described “City in a Park,” has many beautiful parks, such as Bannerwood, Crossroads, Downtown, Highland, Lake Hills, Lakemont, Mercer Slough, Meydenbauer, Robinswood, Surrey Downs, Weowna, and Wilburton Hill. The fact that none of these parks have arterial roads going through them shows Bellevue residents have been prioritizing parks over cars for as long as the city has existed.

Wilburton Hill Park presents a particularly enticing cut-through opportunity to extend 124th Ave south of Main St to the Lake Hills Connector. The City considered this project many years ago, but it was so forcefully rejected by residents that the policy to not do it is now cemented as S-WI-15 in the Wilburton subarea plan .

Downtown Park is another interesting case to examine. Before building that park in the mid 1980s, the City removed a large section of 102nd Avenue, which had bisected the site for decades. As a video from the time makes clear, the City wanted to create a big, green meadow that would last forever, and it would have been unthinkable to compromise that vision for a few seconds of driver convenience.

Downtown Bellevue of the 1980’s, like BelRed today , was a mostly commercial district just beginning its journey to the mixed-use, high-rise urban center it is now. The successful Downtown Park strategy of prioritizing urban green space provides a model worthy of replication in BelRed.

So if Bellevue has never allowed arterials in parks in the past, then why is it planning to do so now? The City laid out the purpose of Spring Boulevard's Zone 3 in an application for a federal grant in 2024. According to the City, the project would:

We dispute the 2-3 minute reduction for drivers. Google Maps estimates the total driving time for the existing route along BelRed Road at just two minutes , so the reduction in driving time would be even less. Also, cars on the new route would often need to yield at crosswalks in the busy park, further eroding any small improvement in driving times.

Apart from that exaggerated driving time reduction, all of the other justifications for the project would also apply to a trail. In fact, if the City wants to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, a trail would be better than a road because it would be more effective at encouraging travel by bicycle without creating the infamous induced traffic demand associated with new roads. And if the City wants to attract investment, a park without an arterial would be more appealing to residents, and therefore more attractive for housing developers and employers.

The Spring Boulevard plan was initially presented to the City Council in 2011. At that time, there were plans for another large park in BelRed . It was tentatively called Northup Meadows, and it would have been on the site of what instead became Sound Transit’s train base . Since the plan for that park fell apart, the other BelRed park (in Spring Boulevard’s path) has gained a new degree of importance as the only park in the rapidly-growing area. It is only appropriate to re-evaluate the need for Spring Boulevard (Zone 3) in light of the significantly changed conditions.
To put our case simply: BelRed Park is a wonderful idea and letting drivers cut through would wreck it.

Parents visiting the park would need to constantly worry about safety as distracted drivers speed by. Their kids couldn’t roam freely and play. Picnicking families would have to put up with constant road noise and backfiring car exhausts. Green grass would cede to hot asphalt. Even with a crosswalk or two, people would try to cross the road everywhere, a recipe for pedestrian injuries. Being close to light rail stations could make BelRed Park one of the best outdoor event spaces in the city, but nobody wants a bunch of loud cars cutting through their event.

Now let’s talk about money. Spring Boulevard's Zone 3 project would cost about $75 million . Last year, Bellevue staff estimated a trail cost at $18-20 million ( on page 12 of these minutes ). In other words, about 75% of the project budget would be directed exclusively at the goal of trying to save drivers a few seconds of travel time.

With a trail, all of the City’s other goals could be achieved at 25% the cost. (Since most of that cost is for land acquisition, and the land owner is Sound Transit , who has been supportive of parks and pedestrian infrastructure around their stations, we might be able to save even more money by making a deal with Sound Transit to put a trail on their land without buying it.)

Think about your favorite park. Now imagine what it would be like with an arterial road going directly through it. That’s what the Spring Boulevard Zone 3 project would do to BelRed Park, before it even has a chance to show how great it can be.

articles.title: Hunter-gatherer societies are often put on a pedestal as paragons of equality – but the reality is more complicated
articles.author:
<name>Duncan Stibbard Hawkes, Assistant Professor of Anthropology, Baylor University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/duncan-stibbard-hawkes-2748866"/>
paras: On the shores of Lake Eyasi in Northern Tanzania, a small number of people still hunt and gather their food. Today a Hadza hunter has taken down an animal – a kudu . He can’t carry it by himself, so he cuts his poisoned arrow from its flank, covers the carcass in dry grass to hide it from hyenas and heads home to enlist help.

News spreads like wildfire across the camp. Everybody rushes to the kill. They divide up the carcass, carry it back, then divvy it up some more. Every family gets some, and after the meat is cooked, there’s more sharing still. On a good day like today, the hunter and his family retain half, but sometimes they keep much less. People may even walk from other camps, and almost everyone, from miles around, is entitled to a share.

The post-hunt scene above is idyllic. It paints a quintessential picture of egalitarianism and equality. But our experience as anthropologists working with the Hadza people of Tanzania and with the Tsimane people of Bolivia’s Amazon rainforest is that inequalities are part of even the most equal of societies. Furthermore, the equalities that do exist often emerge from selfish motives.

Insights like ours are revising researchers’ understanding of both the past and how people operate today, as inequality grows globally . Hunter-gatherers are often at the center of heated academic battles about what it means to be human, including debates over gender , war and peace and whether humans are, by nature, egalitarian or hierarchical .

Sometimes these debates oversimplify. So we pulled together hundreds of different sources covering more than a century of ethnography to find out just how egalitarian hunter-gatherer and other subsistence societies really are.

Anthropologists have called hunter-gatherers such as the Hadza “egalitarian societies,” with equalities of power, wealth and social status . And it’s true that the traditional subsistence communities we work with successfully limit many inequalities.

Most families have similar, modest possessions and store little material wealth . When leaders do emerge, they are highly constrained in how they can direct other people . People often make decisions via consensus, and, if they cannot reach agreement, families will move away.

While the same anthropologists also emphasize that some hunter-gatherers are very unequal and that equality takes deliberate effort , the prevailing impression is that equality characterizes hunter-gatherers, past and present.

A quick trip to your local bookshop will reveal grand claims, including that past hunter-gatherer societies had no permanent leadership and no hierarchy , inequality only spread with the development of agriculture , and humans are noble by nature .

Some scientists are pushing back against these utopian portrayals. The popular bestseller, “ The Dawn of Everything ,” calls egalitarianism a “Garden of Eden narrative” that lacks substance. Other scholars have called egalitarian societies a scientific origin myth .
So where does the truth lie? Probably somewhere in between.
In our recent wide-ranging review of the evidence from the early 20th century onward, we found that no society lacked inequality.

Like the Hadza, the Ju/’Hoansi of the Kalahari desert in southern Africa had little property and widespread food-sharing, yet certain families controlled valuable hunting territory surrounding waterholes . The Bayaka of the central African rainforest had little material inequality, yet they bought, sold and hoarded ritual knowledge . The Philippine Agta controlled and arranged their children’s marriages, hugely discriminating against orphans .

Gender inequalities were commonplace. The Tanzanian Hadza keep certain cuts of meat exclusively for older men , and give more respect to better hunters . Across societies, women have universally done more direct parenting , and men have participated more frequently in community-level decision-making .

No society lacks informal leadership . Age was another source of inequality. In many Australian societies, older men controlled ritual secrets and had power over the marriage choices of younger relatives .

Our study also found that although hunter-gatherers are frequently generous , the processes limiting inequality often do not require any generosity. Instead, equality often results from people’s self-interested motives to acquire resources, status and autonomy.

A great example of this is food-sharing. Although each Hadza family gets a cut of kudu meat, it often happens not because the hunter’s family prioritizes total equality, but because other families request it vociferously. It can involve more taking than giving , often through strongly stated demands or complaints .

Another example is ridicule and mockery of stingy or braggadocious individuals, which keeps greed and bravado in check . Paradoxically, status-seeking can also promote equality, when cooperating to gain status diffuses status throughout the community .
Many of these inequality-reducing processes are familiar to people everywhere.

Ridicule and mockery are ubiquitous in industrialized societies, from political cartoons to social media. Lampooning authority is even common in autocratic societies where governments spend large sums of money suppressing speech . Demands and complaints form the basis of strikes and collective bargaining. And key to social mobility is cooperation among people of different social strata .

Like many great debates, the truth is complex: Our ancient hunter-gatherer ancestors didn’t reach the giddy heights of inequality seen in other societies over the last 6,000 years, but putting hunter-gatherers on a pedestal as paragons of equality is a mistake. Sweeping statements about equality in the past blind us to the tools that probably allowed ancient hunter-gatherers to combat inequality, just as they and people in all societies do today.

Egalitarianism, then, is best seen not as perfect equality but as a set of tools that people use to secure their own autonomy and access to resources. Equality along one dimension or another might be the outcome, but it doesn’t rely on people being amazingly noble or completely lacking in greed or status-seeking. If you consider egalitarianism as equality-creating processes, you can see that it is a widespread reality among hunter-gatherer societies, and beyond.

articles.title: The biggest unresolved question in AI right now, and more takeaways from Madrona’s IA40 Summit
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Executives from companies such as Microsoft, Amazon, Anthropic and Stripe agreed on a lot this week about where AI is headed. But one big question was left unresolved: who keeps the relationship with the customer, and the data that comes from it, once an AI agent is in the middle?

That question was a recurring theme at Madrona’s IA40 Summit , the venture capital firm’s annual gathering of AI startups, investors and tech executives, held Wednesday at the Four Seasons Hotel on the downtown Seattle waterfront.

As Madrona Managing Director Matt McIlwain said in his closing remarks, the question of who gets to use the data that comes from people’s engagement with AI systems came up “over and over and over again” during the day.
GeekWire attended the entire day and came up with these takeaways, reducing our own human bottleneck (see below) with lots of back-and-forth with Anthropic’s Claude and other AI tools.

AI agents are coming between companies and their customers: Charles Lamanna , the Microsoft executive vice president who oversees Microsoft 365 and the platform behind Copilot, predicted most business software will end up being used by AI assistants on a person’s behalf, leaving software makers with less power to set prices.

Jean-Denis Greze , CEO of Town, a startup that makes an AI assistant for work, went further. Since about July, he said, AI has been able to operate a browser or a computer almost as well as a person, at a reasonable cost. That means an AI assistant can work through an app’s user interface the way a person does, without needing an API from the software maker, he said.

“Everything is going to become a thin app because the better the AI gets at using the computer, the less the app matters as a unit of software,” Greze said, echoing the term Lamanna had used that morning for software that people open only briefly.

The same shift is under way in retail. Maia Josebachvili , Stripe’s chief revenue officer for AI, said commerce by AI agents on Stripe was roughly flat for eight or nine months and then rose sharply in the past six weeks.

Many merchants make their money by getting shoppers to add to their orders at checkout and by showing them ads, she said, and they lose those chances when an agent does the buying. That won’t work over the long term, Josebachvili said.
That conflict is playing out in real time in a high-profile dispute between two tech giants. Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse assistant from shopping on its site last month.

The data side of the question came up in a session with Anthropic Chief Technology Officer Rahul Patil . Moderator Raphaëlle d’Ornano asked who owns the record of an AI agent’s work, including its mistakes and corrections, and whether it belongs to the customer. She said she has never gotten a clear answer.
Patil didn’t answer directly. He said each company that supplies the software for running agents will work to improve them, and “will use every data that’s available to them to make it better.”
“It’s good for the ecosystem if the agents actually improve,” he said.

Swami Sivasubramanian , Amazon Web Services’ vice president of Agentic AI and Emerging Technologies, said one of the least appreciated parts of making AI agents work is getting them the right company data for the task.

AWS in June announced a service for that purpose, called AWS Context, which maps the relationships in a company’s data for agents to use. Sivasubramanian said it’s meant to work across platforms and cloud providers, and he expects this kind of service to be a basic building block for the next 20 years, as cloud storage and databases were two decades ago.

Most companies aren’t keeping up with the technology: Patil said Anthropic writes about 200 times as much code as it did 18 months ago. Some customers have doubled or tripled their output, he said, but almost none have seen gains like Anthropic’s.

“The bottleneck is actually not AI. The bottleneck is human,” said Archana Vemulapalli , global head of AI product management at Goldman Sachs. A company’s roles and processes were built before AI, she said.

Sivasubramanian said teams inside Amazon were showing him impressive AI agents they had built in two or three weeks. When he asked when the agents could be rolled out, he said, almost every team told him it still had to work out security, identity and monitoring.
McKinsey senior partner Lari Hamalainen said about 40% of companies say AI has increased their profits, but only 6% describe the increase as substantial.
Even as AI becomes more and more capable, there’s still lots of work to do to close the gap between “the goals, the capabilities, and what we all are aspiring to do,” McIlwain said.

Companies are split on depending on a single AI provider: Anthropic’s Patil, notably, argued that large companies are spending too much effort preserving the ability to switch between AI providers. To keep that option open, he said, they end up building for the least common denominator, limiting themselves to the features every AI model shares. That effort also takes their engineers away from the work that sets their own company apart.

Carlos Guestrin , co-CEO of the AI startup Noeri, offered an alternative take on the same panel. Intelligence shouldn’t be controlled by one or two companies that own the models, he said, and every company should be able to build and own its own AI systems.
Guestrin is a Stanford computer science professor and former University of Washington professor who founded the Seattle machine learning startup Turi, which Apple acquired in 2016 .

Eno Reyes , co-founder and chief technology officer of Factory, a startup that makes AI coding tools, said on a later panel that many businesses don’t see a way to build their future without ceding control to one AI lab. Thomas Dohmke, the former GitHub CEO who now leads the startup Entire, said developers always want choice.

Amazon works with more than one AI lab. It is a major Anthropic investor and partner, and Dan Grossman , Amazon’s vice president of business and corporate development, pointed out on an investor panel that Amazon had launched a managed agents product with OpenAI that week.
Amazon also sells its own product for running AI agents, AgentCore, which overlaps with Anthropic’s Managed Agents.

Companies don’t yet trust AI with important decisions: Zico Kolter , the Carnegie Mellon professor who chairs the safety and security committee of OpenAI’s board, said the ability to control AI systems has to keep pace with their capabilities, which might mean developing them more slowly than is possible.

Sivasubramanian said executives worry about whether an AI agent will always follow their company’s rules and regulations. Companies can keep the creativity of AI models, he said, by pairing them with separate systems that check a model’s work against the company’s rules and catch violations.

The money is concentrated in a few companies: The companies on this year’s IA40 list have raised $410 billion since they were founded, according to Madrona’s data. OpenAI, Anthropic and Databricks account for 92% of it.

Anthropic raised $143 billion of its $161 billion total in the 12 months ending Aug. 15, a figure that includes debt. The company has filed confidentially for an initial public offering and is seeking a valuation of about $2 trillion, Reuters reported this week . Bloomberg reported that it could go public as early as mid-November .
Capital spending by Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta and Apple is projected to rise 74% this year to about $742 billion, according to PitchBook figures Madrona presented.
Lamanna said Microsoft’s heaviest AI users among its software developers are each on track to spend more than $1 million a year on AI usage, even with the company’s internal discount.
Madrona’s closing slide said returns on AI are still early for most of the companies using it but look inevitable based on what the earliest adopters are seeing.

articles.title: Seattle voice AI startup Ultravox, formerly known as Fixie, acquired by Inworld
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: Seattle voice AI startup Ultravox , which launched as Fixie , has been acquired by Inworld for an undisclosed sum.
Ultravox was founded in 2022 by Google and Apple veterans to build a speech model for real-time, natural-sounding AI voice agents.

In perhaps its most whimsical project, the startup launched the HiSanta.ai website in December 2023, allowing users to chat with Santa Claus, who spoke with a British accent, as well as Rudolph, Mrs. Claus and other North Pole notables. The site is no longer active.

The company announced a $17 million seed round in March 2023, and PitchBook put its valuation at $51.46 million at the time. Redpoint Ventures led the round, which included Madrona Venture Group, Zetta Venture Partners, SignalFire, Bloomberg Beta and Kearny Jackson. Current and former executives at Google, Amazon and Apple also invested.
Ultravox has 10 employees, according to LinkedIn. It was unclear whether the entire team would join Inworld, which is based in Mountain View, Calif.
“We’re excited to welcome members of the Ultravox team and continue building the platform,” said Inworld CEO Kylan Gibbs in a statement.
The acquisition will allow Inworld to adopt Ultravox’s technology for managing turn-taking and interruptions in voice conversations with AI, which should improve performance in real-time chats.
Inworld has raised $119.8 million since launching in 2021 and is valued at $515 million, according to PitchBook.

Ultravox co-founder Zach Koch was most recently the company’s CEO. His LinkedIn profile says he is now vice president of product at Shopify. Peter Salas , who joined the company as a software engineer in 2023, is currently listed as chief technology officer.

The startup’s original CEO, Matt Welsh , departed two years ago and is now head of AI systems at defense company Palantir Technologies. Co-founders Hessam Bagherinezhad and Justin Uberti also left, in 2023 and 2024 respectively, and both joined OpenAI.
The release announcing the acquisition said Ultravox customers would be upgraded to Inworld’s Realtime TTS-2 voice technology.

articles.title: Seattle Space Week shines a light on eight problems and prospects for pioneers on the final frontier
articles.author: Alan Boyle
paras: How high can Washington state’s space industry rise?

Preliminary findings suggest that the economic impact of the state’s space sector more than doubled between 2018 and 2022, and nearly doubled again between 2022 and now . But at the same time, some leaders of the space community are questioning whether the Pacific Northwest can keep pace with other regional clusters in, say, Florida, Texas and Colorado.

That good news, bad news situation made headlines this week when Stoke Space CEO Andy Lapsa questioned whether he’d pick the Seattle area as his home base if he had to do it over — just before taking the stage as a member of Gov. Bob Ferguson’s Washington Space Council .

Ferguson isn’t the only elected official trying to make sure the Seattle area keeps up on the space frontier. Dana Ralph, the mayor of Kent, Wash., where Stoke is headquartered, made that clear in her remarks during the kickoff for Seattle Space Week at the Museum of Flight.
“We don’t take you for granted,” said Ralph, addressing a gathering of CEOs, investors and other VIPs. “I want you to hear that out loud: We don’t take you for granted.”

Seattle Space Week — highlighted by Tuesday’s Space Northwest Symposium in Federal Way — provided plenty of opportunities for discussing the challenges facing Washington state’s space ventures. Here are four problems to face, and four prospects to look forward to.

The launch crisis: The availability of launch opportunities has shrunk dramatically . “It’s just crazy how there’s this mismatch between supply and demand right now in the industry,” said Tim Beard, Stoke Space’s chief financial officer. “It’s becoming a crisis.”

One factor is the increased demand for deploying satellite constellations for broadband data services (such as Starlink and Amazon Leo) and for future AI data processing (such as Starcloud, SpaceX’s Starmind and Google’s Project Suncatcher).

Another factor is reduced supply: Blue Origin and United Launch Alliance are dealing with setbacks in their next-generation rocket programs. Meanwhile, SpaceX is talking about phasing out its workhorse Falcon 9 rocket as it makes the transition to Starship. The resulting launch crunch is an industry-wide problem, but it hits Seattle’s satellite ventures especially hard.

The workforce challenge: There’s also a limited supply of skilled technicians and engineers. Bill Bruner, CEO of New Frontier Aerospace, ranks that as his No. 1 challenge. “It’s finding skilled, trained people to do, not just the hard engineering work, but the Grade 13, Grade 14 graduate technical work,” he said. “We need a national solution to that problem.”

Ralph said Kent and other Seattle-area municipalities need to partner with state government and commercial ventures to address the challenge. “We should be able to make it easier for employers to invest in apprenticeship, credentials and on-the-job training,” she said. “We need to build a workforce system that moves with industry, not several years behind it.”

Funding from faraway: Much of the funding that fuels Seattle’s space ventures comes from elsewhere. “There are a lot of VCs in Seattle, but they’re not necessarily space VCs,” said Mike Reilly, chief strategy officer for Varda Space Industries. “I feel like a lot of the space money comes out of L.A. and San Francisco.”

Brian Monnin, co-founder and chief commercial officer at Sophia Space, said midsize space ventures need to find ways to fill their funding gaps. “ Debt financing is one way,” he said. “But I think there should be more public-private combinations of firms, traditional banks working alongside debt financiers, working alongside the public for us to fill that vast middle.”

Regional rivalries: Several executives said other states are much more aggressive than Washington when it comes to attracting space ventures. “The incentives just aren’t here,” Monnin said. “We’re looking at where we build our Factory One for Sophia Space tiles , and you have to look at the incentives from sovereign funds in New Mexico, Louisiana and others. They’re far more attractive than they are in this state currently.”

The inter-regional competition was one of the challenges cited by Stoke Space CEO Andy Lapsa — and by his CFO as well. “I need to be pretty direct in that we’re being actively courted by any number of states: Colorado, Texas, Florida,” Beard said. “They want us to move there, but Washington state is the right place for Stoke. … I hope our policymakers in Olympia, throughout the state, our senators hear this. We want to stay in Washington state. Help us do that.”

Public-private partnerships: The newly announced Washington Space Council isn’t likely to set up a multibillion-dollar fund for space ventures anytime soon, but it could serve as a forum for business executives and government officials to work out realistic ways to foster the state’s space industry.

Will the work of the council go beyond virtue-signaling? Last year, the Governor’s Economic Development Strategic Reserve Fund awarded $350,000 to support Portal Space Systems’ expansion into a 50,000-square-foot satellite manufacturing facility in Bothell, Wash. Such grants may serve as a model for future financial incentives.

Satellite offices: Space ventures don’t need to be headquartered in Washington to benefit the state’s space industry. Cowboy Space, for example, is based in California but recently announced the opening of a 291,035-square-foot spacecraft design and manufacturing facility in Kent . BlackSky is based in Virginia, but its satellites are built in a 22,000-square-foot factory in Tukwila, Wash. SpaceX may have moved its corporate headquarters from California to Texas , but it still makes more than half of the world’s satellites at its facilities in Redmond and Woodinville, Wash.

Just as Google and Meta maintain engineering hubs in the Seattle area, out-of-state satellite ventures are likely to establish Seattle-area outposts. “The fundamentals that made this region are still here: talent, a deep supply chain, industrial capacity, a culture of making things, and generations of knowledge that you simply cannot re-create overnight,” Ralph said.

Coming attractions: The silver lining to the launch crisis is that Stoke Space and other commercial space ventures plan to fill the gap. And when SpaceX’s Starship enters service, that could dramatically change the parameters of the launch market. Ron Faith, CEO of RBC Signals, said this week’s first orbital Starship flight was “a pretty big milestone event.”

“Having Starship go into orbit and deploy real satellites … that’s a significant increase in capacity for launch,” he said. “But with that said, we’re also seeing many, many more launchers come online.” The list includes Blue Origin’s New Glenn , United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan , Rocket Lab’s Neutron , Firefly Aerospace’s Alpha , Relativity Space’s Terran R — and yes, Stoke Space’s Nova .
A pad of our own: When it comes to space facilities, the Seattle area lacks two big items: a nearby NASA center and an orbital launch pad.

During a recent visit to Redmond , NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman didn’t offer much encouragement for the space agency’s fans in the Pacific Northwest. “I think it’s unlikely we’re going to be adding any additional centers right now,” he told me.
But at the Museum of Flight, Ferguson said the Washington Space Council “will look for ways we might be able to develop Washington-based commercial launch capabilities.”

At the Space Northwest Symposium, Monnin wondered why the Seattle area’s space ventures haven’t forged closer ties with the region’s military installations. “It’s a shame that over the last few decades we haven’t seen the affinity toward Fort Lewis-McChord or the naval base in Bremerton as innovation centers … because from an orbital compute standpoint, the biggest need is defense- or security-related,” he said. “How we haven’t tapped into that as a state, I think, is a miss.”

The Pacific Northwest’s geography would make it difficult to put a launch pad in a place that avoids posing a significant risk to populated areas. That’s why Blue Origin and Stoke Space have their orbital launch pads in Florida instead of Washington. But when Beard was asked about the prospect of using a pad closer to home, he wasn’t dismissive.

“Launching from the Washington coast would be fantastic,” he said. “Also, my geography is not great, but I think it’s slightly closer to ship a rocket to the Washington coast than it is all the way down to Cape Canaveral. So, that’s one advantage as well. We’d love to see launch here, and I think that we’d be good partners to do that with.”

articles.title: Op-Ed: Seattle’s Utility Fee Policy Echoes Redlining
articles.author: Donna Breske (Guest Contributor)
paras: Seattle’s permitting policies for new housing requires that applicants pay for public infrastructure upgrades within historically marginalized neighborhoods that are not required of applicants in more affluent neighborhoods.

Redlined communities faced policies, including the denial of access to home loans that restricted home ownership and affordable housing. Two current Seattle permitting policies for new-home construction continue this inequitable treatment.

Despite Seattle’s official commitments on racial justice and social equity, inequitable outcomes are embedded within the sidewalk and water service policies and fees associated with new home construction. The outcome for many marginalized communities is increased costs, which could exceed those in more affluent communities by $350,000 for the same type of project.

The Seattle Municipal Code has a two-tiered sidewalk policy. The code gives relief for housing projects outside of Urban Centers, while no such relief is afforded to the projects within. This relief applies to projects of nine units or less. For those small projects required to install sidewalks, the cost can be upwards of $100,000.

Since Seattle has designated the lion’s share of its Urban Centers in historically “red-lined” communities, there is a social equity disparity that is reflected in the Seattle Sidewalk Code. Relief is provided to more affluent communities, however no such relief to historically marginalized communities.

A better solution may be to change the Seattle Municipal Code to allow the option for payment of a reasonable fee-in-lieu-of sidewalk construction. This will facilitate equitable relief regardless of the location of the project within the City. The money collected could be applied to areas of the city with the highest need for sidewalks.

Another disparity appears in Seattle Public Utilities’ (SPU’s) water-service policy WTR-440. It applies to a water main that runs primarily through historically marginalized communities and is installed within Beacon Avenue and extends north and continues under 21st Avenue S.
The policy requires permit applicants whose property is on a street where the supply main is located to pay for and install a large valve at a total cost around $250,000.

Furthermore, Seattle’s supply main is located within communities that are also designated as Design Review Equity Areas . Outreach to these communities is required to ensure that they have a meaningful voice in projects affecting them. These Design Review Areas coincide with historically redlined areas.

One neighborhood in the North Rainier Urban Hub, has seen five small housing proposals unable to proceed. Numerous projects along Beacon Avenue have come to an abrupt halt once the project proponent is informed of the valve requirement. Small projects have no economy of scale to pay the $250,000 estimated cost. Small-scale homebuilders are not suited to perform major public works water system upgrades and the end result is unrealized housing and ongoing social inequity.

Not all permitting barriers include a social inequity component. Moreover, permitting policies that affect housing outcomes do extend beyond Seattle to many jurisdictions throughout the Puget Sound region.
Barriers run the gamut and include storm water policy, road network, strict floor area ratio requirements that limit housing capacity, critical area interpretations, and more.

articles.title: Scores Turn Out To Celebrate Sound Transit's First Infill Station
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: What had been billed as a "small community event" turned into a major party Wednesday as hundreds of transit fans converged on Sound Transit's newest light rail station in North Seattle to celebrate its grand opening. Pinehurst Station , perched over I-5 near NE 130th Street, is the agency's first infill station, a stop added along an existing line.

"It was a joyous occasion with people walking, biking, and rolling to check out their new mobility option, including many arriving on King County Metro's new Route 77, which provides a direct and convenient connection to the station," Sound Transit CEO Dow Constantine said the following day at a board committee meeting.

Sound Transit had undeniably treated the opening of Pinehurst Station as a subdued affair, in the wake of full line openings where the agency pulled out all the stops. Unlike past major light rail openings, the start of service happened on a weekday, meeting the agency's promise of getting the station open in the third quarter of the year. A ribbon cutting occurred the night before, separating the elected officials celebrating the station from the throngs of riders checking it out.

Just one food truck was on hand to provide sustenance for hundreds, at a station that is fairly isolated from other restaurants, and the Sound Transit pop-up shop on hand selling custom Pinehurst merch started running out of inventory fairly quickly.

But none of that seemed to faze transit lovers who converged on the station plaza by the hundreds, with many standing in an epic line that stretched back to 130th Street for a chance to win a Boop collectible. (Don't know Boop? You've been missing out. )

Other attendees listened to live music or participated in art making activities with Romson Bustillo, the very same artist who created the artwork adorning Pinehurst Station – porcelain enamel paintings that wrap around the side of the building into its main entrance from 130th. Bustillo's booth was popular with kids who could make their own art projects to take home as souvenirs.

But most who stopped by were there to check out the station itself, which had originally not been set to open until 2031, moved up in order to take advantage of the ability to do work concurrently with the broader Lynnwood Link extension. While that line ultimately beat Pinehurst to a ribbon-cutting by more than two years, the ability to do work before that happened ultimately saved riders headaches in addition to being cheaper for Sound Transit.

As Sound Transit's festival wrapped up, a group of around 50 joined for The Urbanist's walking tour of the neighborhood. The tour used the Jackson Park Perimeter Trail to explore the fenced edge of the golf course, before turning south on 15th Avenue NE to visit the fledgling business district. The tour turned back toward the station via NE 125th Street to take in the new protected bike lane and roundabout intersection with Roosevelt Way.

Along the way, James Wu and Shirley Leung of EcoCity Action told tour participants about their group's campaign to reimagine Jackson Park Golf Course . One core idea: making it possible for people to walk through the 160-acre park and get more use out it, such as by adding picnic areas or soccer pitches or basketball courts. Some have even proposed housing , although that's not part of the current campaign given obstacles like zoning and restrictions on reusing park land.

Pinehurst organizer Renee Staton recounted the history of local grassroots advocacy that forced the station into agency plans and accelerated its timeline. Staton said most of her neighbors support the City's plan to upzone Pinehurst's single family areas to allow more housing, and she's pushing to move up the timeline ahead of delayed Comprehensive Plan changes.

Pinehurst has attracted attention for its price tag – $240 million, up from an initial 2020 estimate of $144 million – and its adjacent land use, primarily single-family homes, I-5, and a large, city-owned golf course. One-term Sammamish councilmember (and talk radio host) John Curley called the station a " a total waste of money " and asserted its construction was "criminal."

On the low end, Pinehurst is expected to see around 1,100 daily riders, increasing to as many as 4,200 as Sound Transit fully builds out its light rail network, and the City of Seattle hopefully brings in some additional residential density onto the surrounding blocks.

While Seattle urbanists would certainly love to see Pinehurst embedded into a highrise district, that's not what exists between Northgate and South Shoreline today. When so often the argument around adding density comes up, a lack of infrastructure is cited as a reason to back away, and yet when the infrastructure comes first, it becomes a waste of money.

As far as costs go, it's undeniable that the station is pricey. But as an infill station along an elevated line, $240 million is a steal relative to other Sound Transit projects, only a little more than the at-grade Graham Street infill station in the Rainier Valley at $214 million. The elevated Boeing Access Road Station in Tukwila, so expensive that it was not able to fit into Sound Transit's newly aligned ST3 plan after adjustments were made to account for a $34.5 billion shortfall, is expected to cost as much as $475 million .

One of the biggest value adds right now from Pinehurst come from its ability to act as a bus transfer spot, easier for Metro to access from neighborhoods like Lake City and Bitter Lake than either Shoreline South or Northgate. NE 130th Street, being remade right now by the Seattle Department of Transportation to feature protected bike lanes connecting right with the station, is much improved from its state just a few years ago.

Haters going to hate, but ultimately allowing riders in 2026 to access Pinehurst Station, years ahead of schedule, is a major win for transit in Puget Sound. And the crowds that turned out Wednesday to celebrate the day are a testament to that fact.

articles.title: Friday Roundtable: Salmon SEEson
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: Every year, thousands of salmon travel though creeks, rivers and lakes in King County on their return trip from the ocean. These adult salmon return to fresh water to spawn the next generation. The county’s Salmon SEEson program, now in its 20th year, highlights the habitat restoration, stormwater management, and community stewardship that ensure the fish can complete their journey. The program also highlights some of the best locations for watching the great salmon migration. An interactive map is available here .

One of the primary dangers to coho salmon in King County’s streams and rivers is a chemical from car tires . A chemical called 6PPD is used in almost all tires to protect them from ground-level ozone. When ozone reacts with 6PPD, it creates a toxic chemical called 6PPD-quinone. 6PPD-quinone is left on the roadway and washed into nearby waterways during the next rain. Some locations have a stormwater filter to prevent 6PPD-quinone from entering a waterway, but these systems cannot be built for every road.

To avoid adding more 6PPD-quinone to the salmon’s habitat, do not drive to see the salmon migration. Instead, ride the bus! EcoCity Action has organized a few transit trips to see salmon. articles.title: Kink Center wants Capitol Hill to know it’s mostly about the ‘center’
articles.author: AGPhoto
paras: Walk past the E Pike sidewalk sign for Kink Center and you might expect something out of a dirty movie.
Step inside on a typical night and you’re more likely to find a board game in progress, a book club mid-debate, or somebody passing around cupcakes.
“I think that people see these opening scenes of The Matrix as the idea for what a kink club looks like,” said Luna , the volunteer-run venue’s director of marketing.
“… and we’re just in here eating cupcakes.”

That gap between expectation and reality is kind of the point. Kink Center opened last year as what its organizers call a third space, a community center first, oriented toward kink and queer folks and built around accessibility.

Executive director Raven Dubh says the idea grew out of need. Seattle has some good options for kink events, but few built around the accessibility the team wanted, and almost none affordable enough for a beginning organizer to take a swing.
“It’s a very expensive failure if you try somewhere else,” Dubh said.
Dubh said friends trying to organize their own events ran into cost and resource challenges.
“The more I was trying to help people do that, I realized they couldn’t,” Dubh said. “They couldn’t front that kind of money.”
Accessibility at the center takes many forms: masking and clean-air policies with HEPA filtration, ADA-accessible bathrooms and elevator access, rental rates kept low so tickets can be cheap or free.
“The barrier to entry is so low, and so many people can try, and the cost if it doesn’t work out isn’t so high for them,” Luna said.

Most of what happens here is about getting together and talking. Socials fill the bulk of the calendar, Luna said, followed by classes, “We found a really big thirst to learn in the community”, and then parties, including the center’s own Masked Mayhem. Outside groups rent the space for everything from kink events to birthday parties to company holiday parties, as long as they follow the venue’s posted guidelines.

Neighbors, by the team’s account, have been supportive. Luna said the center has a good relationship with nearby businesses, including downstairs neighbor A/stir it taps for catering. And on a Hill that’s also home to shops like Doghouse Leathers , the sign out front rarely raises eyebrows.
“People see the Kink Center sign, and maybe they don’t frequent Cap Hill,” Luna said. “And they just go, ‘That’s Cap Hill.'”
Luna sees the center as a natural extension of the neighborhood’s queer, sex-positive history.
For Dubh, it’s about normalizing. “It’s not an us versus them,” Dubh said. “It’s a part of that person’s life, and as much as we can normalize that into society, that should be our north star.”
That’s why the calendar includes book clubs and meetups that have little to do with kink.
“When we say third space for kink people, that’s what we mean,” Dubh said. “There are things you can do here because you are part of a community. It doesn’t have to be kink.”

Kink Center is volunteer-run and furnished almost entirely with donated furniture. Dubh, who works in tech, has covered much of the gap personally. This year, the center shifted to asking for small monthly donations, $1 or $2, which made budgeting more predictable. Dubh said the amount they cover out of pocket each month has dropped “pretty dramatically.”
“Every dollar counts,” Dubh said, including the couple of bucks folks donate at events.

The next goal is expanding into the other half of the building. The current layout limits most events around 50 to 75 people. Opening the wall would allow 100-person classes, cheaper tickets, better pay for educators, and events the current shape can’t fit.
“We sell out a lot of our classes, and we wish we could just have an extra 20 or 30 seats,” Dubh said. What’s holding it back? “It’s just money.”

Who’s behind it? The answer, Luna said, is regular people, including volunteers who work the door for an hour and head home, “because all they wanted to do was help at the door for an hour and contribute to their community in that way.”

Dubh said the team’s queerness shows up in how decisions get made: varied backgrounds, ideas Dubh never would have reached alone, and directors empowered to push back. Dubh doesn’t even want to stay on the board long-term. “I want to be punted out so fast,” Dubh said.

Luna said the table feels level. “Grace is always given because we are all focused and aligned on the same goal, which is providing a space to the community that is accessible and feels good for everybody.”

For the kink-curious, both recommend starting small with a social or a munch, like the board game munch the center hosts twice a month. Dubh said the Seattle Freeze actually works in newcomers’ favor.
“If you go to an event and just don’t socialize, it’s kind of expected,” Dubh said. “You just existed in the space, and that is a big step one.”
“Everyone was new once,” Luna said. “That’s what we’re all doing this for.”
“Kink Center as a name, it’s actually backwards in terms of our priority,” Dubh said. “Third space first.”
Kink Center is located at 816 E Pike. Learn more at kinkcenter.org .

articles.title: 12th and Pike reopens as city wraps up main construction on longer than expected sewer overhaul
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: The intersection when it was still fully under repair (Image: CHS)

Seattle Public Utilities has provided an update on the much longer and much more involved than planned construction project and street closures at 12th and Pike, telling CHS crews have completed the main construction phase of the major sewer repair project.
CHS reported last month on neighborhood business and community concerns around the long closure and the Seattle Department of Transportation’s handling of prolonged city street closures.

The project is also a symptom of how the city tends to some of its largest infrastructure needs, pushing back timelines due to budget and schedule considerations as significant problems from aging pipes only get worse. The summer construction timeline on the 12th and Pike project had to be doubled to six weeks of closures after excavation crews ran into unmapped wiring, old concrete, and tangled utility lines.

In the SPU update provided to CHS Friday morning, SPU says the intersection has been “officially” reopened to traffic. Restoration work on sidewalks and ADA ramps will continue through late October, running during adjusted off-peak hours (9 AM to 3 PM) and temporarily pausing from October 2 to October 4 for the nearby Elysian Brewing Great Pumpkin Festival .
Through the final phase, SPU says the intersection and pedestrian storefront access will remain open, with most street parking available.

articles.title: 911 | Garbage truck driver hospitalized in possible poppers hazmat incident on Harvard Ave E
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: See something others should know about? Email CHS or call/txt (206) 399-5959 . You can view recent CHS 911 coverage here. Hear sirens and wondering what’s going on? Check out reports from @jseattle or join and check in with neighbors in the CHS Facebook Group .
Poppers hazmat incident? Either somebody improperly disposed of a stash of poppers or a neighborhood chemist tossed an experiment into the Capitol Hill trash.

One person was taken to the hospital after Seattle Fire was called to Harvard and Mercer Thursday afternoon for a hazardous materials response when a garbage truck compacted its load “and a potentially hazardous material was released,” an SFD spokesperson tells CHS.

According to Seattle Fire, the truck driver was evaluated by medics and transported in stable condition to the hospital after being exposed to the resulting vapors. The HazMat team determined the spill and localized fumes no longer posed an active threat and cleared the vehicle, while Seattle Public Utilities coordinated on-scene to arrange safe disposal of the contaminated load.
A spokesperson initially told CHS the substance was identified as “Isobutyl Nitrate,” though CHS is checking for clarification.
A far more likely culprit is isobutyl nitrite, the chemical compound widely distributed in sex shops, nightlife venues, and online delivery networks as poppers.

While isobutyl nitrate (with an a) is a heavy industrial additive and chemical reagent, isobutyl nitrite (with an i) is an over-the-counter recreational inhalant that can also induce blood pressure drops, dizziness, and headaches.
If our hunch is correct, a stash of isobutyl made its way into the trash, got smashed, and gave the driver a jolt and scare.
We’ll update when SFD provides final identification details.

Broadway/Pike assault : Police and Seattle Fire were called to the service station at Broadway and Pike early Monday morning to a report of a fight with multiple people involving possible bias. Seattle Fire says it treated one person at the scene of the just after 2:30 AM incident who was transported to the hospital with injuries from the assault. Police rushed to the scene after reports of the large fight and arriving officers reported several people fleeing the area. There were no reported arrests. SPD was not able to provide additional information about the assault or possible hate elements.

Political tire slashing alleged: The Seattle Police Department was investigating a felony harassment incident after responding to the Broadway Dick’s Drive-In Sunday where a driver told officers an unknown attacker slashed her car’s tires and charged at her with a knife in a dispute over her political beliefs. The suspect fled and was not caught at the scene. Officers noted that security footage from neighboring business cameras could only be accessed during regular business hours for follow-up investigation. There were no reported injuries and no immediate arrests.

paras: Happy anniversary. It has been 10 years since we divorced. Cheers to us not working out.

articles.title: The Wages of Whiteness
articles.author: Charles Mudede
paras: Let us leave Seattle and visit Arkansas. The governor of this deep red state is, of course, Sarah Huckabee Sanders. She ran a tight ship as a conservative: pro-life, pro-business, pro-white Christian nationalism, pro-tax cuts (four in a row ). She even rolled back “a number of child labor protections across the state.” No one could doubt her red credentials. She was the real deal, top to bottom. And her bid for a second term in office was pretty much a matter of course.

Then she made one big blunder. Sanders produced a campaign ad that attacked welfare recipients as lazy, as people who could work but chose not to. She declared, like the voice of God from a cloud: “If you’re young, healthy, and get government assistance, you should work, go to school, or volunteer.” Well and good. The problem is this: Her model of a welfare recipient was a young white man playing video games with a VR headset, throwing puffy orange snacks into the void of his mouth, and his body swallowed by a well-worn bean bag in a room that has not seen sunlight in ages.

Her base erupted. What the fuck was she thinking: a white man as a welfare queen? They had enough of this sort of thing, this relentless hating on white males. They’re not lazy. They work hard and are worth far more to society than you know who. All of this is on X . One comment after another: “This is blood libel and should be retracted with a full apology,” “I don’t care if her opponent is Stalin, I would vote for that over this insufferable b*tch,” “…what racial group uses the most public assistance per capita?” “It so fucked up that Dems literally want to kill White men and Republicans run [ads] like this.” One post even has a graph showing the net value of ethnic groups in terms of federal tax revenue: whites: + $1 trillion; Blacks: – 600 billion. And because it’s X, the n-word is used with complete abandon. What a shit show.

But all of this gives us an opportunity to ask an important question: What is this rage really about? Sure, one can say it’s a few racists doing their thing, but it’s much more than that. The Republican Party is, after all, America’s white party. In fact, 66 percent of whites with no advanced education voted for Trump. Meaning, a class of people who would only get a few crumbs–if that–from the golden table of the self-centered billionaire decided he was their savior. How is this possible? The answer is the “psychological wage.”

We owe this curious expression to one of the greatest Black American thinkers of the 20th century, W. E. B. Du Bois. In his exhaustive 1935 book, Black Reconstruction in America , he asks how is it possible that working-class Blacks and whites, a group that has more in common than those in the classes above them, “are kept so far apart that neither sees anything of common interest”? His answer: the psychological wage.

Du Bois writes: “It must be remembered that the white group of laborers, while they received a low wage, were compensated in part by a sort of public and psychological wage . They were given public deference and titles of courtesy because they were white. They were admitted freely [to various restricted amenities and milieu] with all classes of white people. The police were drawn from their ranks, and the courts, dependent upon their votes, treated them with such leniency as to encourage lawlessness. Their vote selected public officials, and while this had small effect upon the economic situation, it had great effect upon their personal treatment and the deference shown them.”

What Du Bois is getting here is of great importance. There’s the wage that everyone gets if they have a job. But there’s this other phantom thing called the psychological wage, which, in the US, is only handed to poor and working whites. This second wage makes all the difference. It diminishes the value of the first wage to such an extent that it barely needs to rise. It can remain low as long as a white person is proud to be white, as long as they see themselves represented in houses of power, on corporate boards, in the top ranks of the army, in statues on statehouse lawns. And most important of all, if others, particularly Black people, are seen to suffer in some way because of their color. Those in power must always perform this function: make a display of humiliating, belittling, denigrating Black and brown people. This is why Trump is back in the White House.

This is also why so many in Sanders’s base are furious at her. The campaign ads’ depiction of a lazy white man violated the agreement between them and their white betters. Furthermore, she diminished the value of the psychological wage at a time when they really need it, at a time when real wages are not only very low but, as inflation and, consequently, the cost of living rises, are also falling in value.

A person on X had this to say, after reading the comments to Sanders’s ad: “LOL. how do you all turn something that wasn’t racist into something racist?” Du Bois gave us the answer nearly 100 years ago.
